query: Hey folks - been hearing some chatter about new regulations around offshore support teams and AI disclosures. What's the latest on that? Need to understand if this impacts our roadmap and whether we need to loop in legal.
chunk_content:
:rotating_light: *Legislation Alert for CX & Support Leaders*
The _Keep Call Centers in America Act (S. 2495)_ was recently introduced in Congress. On the surface, it’s framed as protecting U.S. jobs and increasing transparency. But for those of us running customer support operations, I can’t help but feel this is a step too far.
Here’s why:
• The bill would require companies to disclose whether an interaction is handled by a *U.S.-based agent, offshore agent, or AI* — and give customers the right to request transfer to a U.S. human.
• Companies outsourcing could land on a *public list for 5 years*, with restrictions on federal contracts, loans, or grants.
• A *120-day notice* to the Dept. of Labor would be required before moving call center work overseas.
As someone leading in this space, I’m frustrated. To me, what matters most is *resolution, speed, and empathy* — not whether the person (or AI) helping me sits in Phoenix, Manila, or Dublin. Adding compliance layers feels like government overreach that doesn’t actually improve customer experience.
:point_right: Am I alone in thinking this? Do consumers really care about agent location or AI disclosure as long as they get their issue solved promptly and politely?
Would love to hear how others in CX and support are viewing this — and whether you see this as a real risk, a symbolic bill, or something we need to prepare to adapt to.
validation_reason: The message directly addresses the query about new regulations around offshore support teams and AI disclosures by detailing the Keep Call Centers in America Act (S. 2495), which requires disclosure of whether support is handled by US-based agents, offshore agents, or AI. The message outlines specific regulatory requirements that would impact support operations and roadmaps, making it highly relevant to the original question.

IMHO, it really shouldn't matter where the agent sits. True, I'd like disclosure if I'm working with an AI, and have the option to "escalate to a human."

There are already many laws in this area:
GDPR already worries about where your data is stored.
FedRAMP and similar already dictate who can access info on government-related accounts.

But (afaik) you normally wouldn't know (other than accents) whether a call-center person with whom you are talking is located in the US or elsewhere. And, if in the US, you don't know whether they are sitting at home, in a fancy corporate building, or are in prison. (I don't know if this is still so, but I think many call centers used prison labor years ago.)

IMHO, it really shouldn't matter where the agent sits. True, I'd like disclosure if I'm working with an AI, and have the option to "escalate to a human."

There are already many laws in this area:
GDPR already worries about where your data is stored.
FedRAMP and similar already dictate who can access info on government-related accounts.

But (afaik) you normally wouldn't know (other than accents) whether a call-center person with whom you are talking is located in the US or elsewhere. And, if in the US, you don't know whether they are sitting at home, in a fancy corporate building, or are in prison. (I don't know if this is still so, but I think many call centers used prison labor years ago.)

And would this extend to email, chat, and text? Or just voice?

And - can I have separate Support plans? Plan A is you get whomever we send your issue to, 24x7 (or 24x5). Plan B is you only get US-based agents, but Plan B costs more than Plan A for obvious reasons, and is only 12x5.
validation_reason: The message directly addresses the query about compliance requirements for disclosing support team location. What I'm looking for: Has anyone in this channel documented specific operational frameworks or customer communication strategies for organizations that need to balance federal contracting requirements with global workforce distribution? Specifically:

1. Precedent-setting approaches for customer expectations regarding service delivery models

query: Hey folks, quick question - wasn't there something posted recently about new legislation that could affect our offshore support team? I remember seeing a thread but can't find it now. Something about having to disclose agent locations to customers?
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
:rotating_light: *Legislation Alert for CX & Support Leaders*
The _Keep Call Centers in America Act (S. 2495)_ was recently introduced in Congress. On the surface, it’s framed as protecting U.S. jobs and increasing transparency. But for those of us running customer support operations, I can’t help but feel this is a step too far.
Here’s why:
• The bill would require companies to disclose whether an interaction is handled by a *U.S.-based agent, offshore agent, or AI* — and give customers the right to request transfer to a U.S. human.
• Companies outsourcing could land on a *public list for 5 years*, with restrictions on federal contracts, loans, or grants.
• A *120-day notice* to the Dept. of Labor would be required before moving call center work overseas.
As someone leading in this space, I’m frustrated. To me, what matters most is *resolution, speed, and empathy* — not whether the person (or AI) helping me sits in Phoenix, Manila, or Dublin. Adding compliance layers feels like government overreach that doesn’t actually improve customer experience.
:point_right: Am I alone in thinking this? Do consumers really care about agent location or AI disclosure as long as they get their issue solved promptly and politely?
Would love to hear how others in CX and support are viewing this — and whether you see this as a real risk, a symbolic bill, or something we need to prepare to adapt to.

[Reply by unknown]
IMHO, it really shouldn't matter where the agent sits. True, I'd like disclosure if I'm working with an AI, and have the option to "escalate to a human."

There are already many laws in this area:
GDPR already worries about where your data is stored.
FedRAMP and similar already dictate who can access info on government-related accounts.

But (afaik) you normally wouldn't know (other than accents) whether a call-center person with whom you are talking is located in the US or elsewhere. And, if in the US, you don't know whether they are sitting at home, in a fancy corporate building, or are in prison. (I don't know if this is still so, but I think many call centers used prison labor years ago.)

And would this extend to email, chat, and text? Or just voice?

And - can I have separate Support plans? Plan A is you get whomever we send your issue to, 24x7 (or 24x5). Plan B is you only get US-based agents, but Plan B costs more than Plan A for obvious reasons, and is only 12x5.

[Reply by unknown]
Same! Just seems like unnecessary overreach and complexity. I just want my issues resolved.

[Reply by unknown]
Absolutely agree. While I understand the goal of boosting U.S. job growth, the operational hurdles would lead to less effective support and a more costly product.

I could see the request to transfer to a US agent playing out something like _“If you’re comfortable speaking with AI, international, or U.S.-based agents, your wait time will be X. If you prefer to speak specifically with a U.S.-based agent, your wait time will be 5X.”_

[Reply by unknown]
Yes, you can have US if you want, but be prepared to wait.

[Reply by unknown]
What I think might happen instead is by in large the customer doesn’t care as long as the issue is resolved, but if the customer doesn’t like the answer they receive the request would be not necessarily “I want to talk to your manager”, it’ll be “I want to talk to someone in the US”. 

The Act isn’t about protecting jobs, it’s more closely aligned with keeping perfectly capable individuals from doing their jobs. It encourages people to make assumptions about competence based on accents and locations, instead of normalizing help. 

[Reply by unknown]
You’re not alone. If this moves forward, treat it as routing and transparency. Say who’s helping up front, default to the fastest capable path, and honor “US human” on request with a clear ETA. Then publish resolution time and CSAT by lane so the data settles the debate.

[Reply by unknown]
Considering that it is being driven by the <https://cwa-union.org/about|CWA> - it makes sense why it would be so focused on pushing for the outcomes they are - and considering <https://www.citizen.org/article/during-trump-presidency-200000-jobs-offshored-and-corporations-involved-awarded-425-billion-in-federal-contracts/|promises back in 2020> by the administration it does seem to be something that was on the agenda but contradicted.

As one in a EU company with no offshoring (but thinking about this in the future) - take what I have to say with a grain of salt. -but I do agree with <@UGFBLDDB4> - while it may focus on the surface of protecting US jobs - it only further reinforces the assumptions and profiling based on location which causes a deeper rift in combination with the recent regulation changes in DEIB laws across the US.

In my personal opinion - it misses the mark in terms of a globally-focused world where much of the world today operates across borders.

Operationally - I agree with <@U03EWLT5NF8> - and what was said before. Set a clear precedent and expectations for customers - give them the option to choose quick with an understanding of what will be different in their experience route them quick - and segment the reporting

:rotating_light: *Legislation Alert for CX & Support Leaders*
The _Keep Call Centers in America Act (S. 2495)_ was recently introduced in Congress. On the surface, it’s framed as protecting U.S. jobs and increasing transparency. But for those of us running customer support operations, I can’t help but feel this is a step too far.
Here’s why:
• The bill would require companies to disclose whether an interaction is handled by a *U.S.-based agent, offshore agent, or AI* — and give customers the right to request transfer to a U.S. human.
• Companies outsourcing could land on a *public list for 5 years*, with restrictions on federal contracts, loans, or grants.
• A *120-day notice* to the Dept. of Labor would be required before moving call center work overseas.
As someone leading in this space, I’m frustrated. To me, what matters most is *resolution, speed, and empathy* — not whether the person (or AI) helping me sits in Phoenix, Manila, or Dublin. Adding compliance layers feels like government overreach that doesn’t actually improve customer experience.
:point_right: Am I alone in thinking this? Do consumers really care about agent location or AI disclosure as long as they get their issue solved promptly and politely?
Would love to hear how others in CX and support are viewing this — and whether you see this as a real risk, a symbolic bill, or something we need to prepare to adapt to.

:rotating_light: *Legislation Alert for CX & Support Leaders*
The _Keep Call Centers in America Act (S. 2495)_ was recently introduced in Congress. On the surface, it’s framed as protecting U.S. jobs and increasing transparency. But for those of us running customer support operations, I can’t help but feel this is a step too far.
Here’s why:
• The bill would require companies to disclose whether an interaction is handled by a *U.S.-based agent, offshore agent, or AI* — and give customers the right to request transfer to a U.S. human.
• Companies outsourcing could land on a *public list for 5 years*, with restrictions on federal contracts, loans, or grants.
• A *120-day notice* to the Dept. of Labor would be required before moving call center work overseas.
As someone leading in this space, I’m frustrated. To me, what matters most is *resolution, speed, and empathy* — not whether the person (or AI) helping me sits in Phoenix, Manila, or Dublin. Adding compliance layers feels like government overreach that doesn’t actually improve customer experience.
:point_right: Am I alone in thinking this? Do consumers really care about agent location or AI disclosure as long as they get their issue solved promptly and politely?
Would love to hear how others in CX and support are viewing this — and whether you see this as a real risk, a symbolic bill, or something we need to prepare to adapt to.

[Message by unknown at 66f93d34-91b4-5e4c-bf26-706358451d82]
You need both depth and breadth. 

It’s difficult to anticipate knowledge coverage across both dimensions, and frankly, it’s easier to measure the gaps.

We developed something we call the *Deflection Gap*, which evaluates knowledge failures across three dimensions:

• *Coverage* – the knowledge is missing.
• *Comprehension* – the knowledge is presented but not aligned to the reader’s skill level (they don’t understand it).
• *Confidence* – the topic is covered and understood, but the reader doesn’t trust it without human confirmation.
These three categories capture the primary reasons for knowledge failures and highlight where to focus improvements in knowledge quality, trust, and coverage.

---

[Message by unknown at 0e26387d-4a11-5769-bf9b-41e8566471b1]
Teams trying to scale AI in support often run into the same trade-off: breadth vs depth of knowledge.

Breadth = pull in every source — tickets, Confluence, forums, product docs, even internal runbooks.
	•	The model gets more detail than customers normally see.
	•	Accuracy improves quickly, but…
	•	Conflicts between sources lead to contradictory answers.
	•	You have to pick which corpus “wins.”
	•	Latency and token costs rise as the context window fills.

Depth = focus only on customer-facing KBs.
	•	Customers get consistent, governed answers.
	•	Lower risk of hallucinations or internal-only content slipping through.
	•	But governance slows down implementation.
	•	Coverage gaps remain, limiting AI accuracy gains in the short run.

Both approaches have real trade-offs:
	•	Breadth speeds time-to-market but risks noise, conflicts, and cost.
	•	Depth builds trust and control but delays measurable AI improvement.

Is there an industry standard, evidence-based approach — measuring how different choices actually affect accuracy, customer trust, and speed to market, instead of assuming more knowledge (or cleaner knowledge) will automatically fix the problem.

When you’ve rolled out AI or self-service, did you start with breadth, depth, or something in between?  How did you decide between these trade offs?

[Message by unknown at 66f93d34-91b4-5e4c-bf26-706358451d82]
You need both depth and breadth. 

It’s difficult to anticipate knowledge coverage across both dimensions, and frankly, it’s easier to measure the gaps.

We developed something we call the *Deflection Gap*, which evaluates knowledge failures across three dimensions:

• *Coverage* – the knowledge is missing.
• *Comprehension* – the knowledge is presented but not aligned to the reader’s skill level (they don’t understand it).
• *Confidence* – the topic is covered and understood, but the reader doesn’t trust it without human confirmation.
These three categories capture the primary reasons for knowledge failures and highlight where to focus improvements in knowledge quality, trust, and coverage.

[Message by unknown at 0e26387d-4a11-5769-bf9b-41e8566471b1]
Teams trying to scale AI in support often run into the same trade-off: breadth vs depth of knowledge.

Breadth = pull in every source — tickets, Confluence, forums, product docs, even internal runbooks.
	•	The model gets more detail than customers normally see.
	•	Accuracy improves quickly, but…
	•	Conflicts between sources lead to contradictory answers.
	•	You have to pick which corpus “wins.”
	•	Latency and token costs rise as the context window fills.

Depth = focus only on customer-facing KBs.
	•	Customers get consistent, governed answers.
	•	Lower risk of hallucinations or internal-only content slipping through.
	•	But governance slows down implementation.
	•	Coverage gaps remain, limiting AI accuracy gains in the short run.

Both approaches have real trade-offs:
	•	Breadth speeds time-to-market but risks noise, conflicts, and cost.
	•	Depth builds trust and control but delays measurable AI improvement.

Is there an industry standard, evidence-based approach — measuring how different choices actually affect accuracy, customer trust, and speed to market, instead of assuming more knowledge (or cleaner knowledge) will automatically fix the problem.

When you’ve rolled out AI or self-service, did you start with breadth, depth, or something in between?  How did you decide between these trade offs?

Ultimately these things are a test of the tipping point of the power balance. Whether they are aware of what they are doing or not, they are investigating your capacity to jump through hoops without question. If you're not happy with it, you won't be happy with the day to day work either. If you aren't going to blindly follow orders, they will probably pick someone who will.

It's almost certainly a waste of time anyway since the majority of hirings are via introduction in the first place and the candidate who already has someone backing them won't be asked to do the task in most cases. The role of the people who cold apply is to be a yardstick, benchmarking for the salary of the chosen person and a reference point in terms of skills and ability and experience.

I think this is why I really hate it, it's deliberately using excessive time of people who are just trying to do work and pay bills, dangling a glimmer of opportunity just out of reach.

For me it's a straight "thanks but no thanks" but I get why people feel they aren't able to do that. I don't think I know anyone who went through rounds of making a video, or worse still doing a task, and actually got a job at the end of it.

Ultimately these things are a test of the tipping point of the power balance. Whether they are aware of what they are doing or not, they are investigating your capacity to jump through hoops without question. If you're not happy with it, you won't be happy with the day to day work either. If you aren't going to blindly follow orders, they will probably pick someone who will.

It's almost certainly a waste of time anyway since the majority of hirings are via introduction in the first place and the candidate who already has someone backing them won't be asked to do the task in most cases. The role of the people who cold apply is to be a yardstick, benchmarking for the salary of the chosen person and a reference point in terms of skills and ability and experience.

I think this is why I really hate it, it's deliberately using excessive time of people who are just trying to do work and pay bills, dangling a glimmer of opportunity just out of reach.

For me it's a straight "thanks but no thanks" but I get why people feel they aren't able to do that. I don't think I know anyone who went through rounds of making a video, or worse still doing a task, and actually got a job at the end of it.

Ultimately these things are a test of the tipping point of the power balance. Whether they are aware of what they are doing or not, they are investigating your capacity to jump through hoops without question. If you're not happy with it, you won't be happy with the day to day work either. If you aren't going to blindly follow orders, they will probably pick someone who will.

It's almost certainly a waste of time anyway since the majority of hirings are via introduction in the first place and the candidate who already has someone backing them won't be asked to do the task in most cases. The role of the people who cold apply is to be a yardstick, benchmarking for the salary of the chosen person and a reference point in terms of skills and ability and experience.

I think this is why I really hate it, it's deliberately using excessive time of people who are just trying to do work and pay bills, dangling a glimmer of opportunity just out of reach.

For me it's a straight "thanks but no thanks" but I get why people feel they aren't able to do that. I don't think I know anyone who went through rounds of making a video, or worse still doing a task, and actually got a job at the end of it.

•Actioning all requests when there’s more than one
•Helping agents understand the importance of answering every question and ensuring the information is correct

•Matching the customer’s tone (especially when it comes to empathizing)
•Actioning all requests when there’s more than one
•Helping agents understand the importance of answering every question and ensuring the information is correct

So far, I’ve tried training sessions, refreshers, having them explain the metrics themselves, breaking down issues, roleplays, and working on examples together. I’ve also used guided questions to help them identify mistakes and challenge what they know, rather than spoon-feeding the answers. These approaches have helped somewhat, but I’m still not seeing consistent results.

Thanks in advance for any tips you can share! I’d love to hear what’s worked for you and your teams to help build consistency and confidence in email responses. :thinking_face2:

Hi all, this is my first post here (took me a bit of courage to hit send), but this feels like the best place to ask about something we’re currently trying to solve: *user reviews. The question is: Has anyone here actively worked on getting user reviews as part of their support or CX work?* What helped you get more of them - and what didn’t?

For more context - at Datamolino, we’ve seen how much genuine reviews help build trust with new customers. But asking for them (and getting them) isn’t easy. In our case, it works best when we’ve built a personal connection - usually after a good support interaction or following a high NPS score. We also thought about offering something in return - not vouchers, but maybe planting a tree as a thank-you. Still, it’s a sensitive area. We want it to feel real, not transactional.

So if you’ve tried anything - campaigns, small nudges, or even experiments that didn’t go as planned - please let me know as I'm looking for honest ideas and inspiration from those who’ve been through this. Thanks so much!

<@U06KXK42HNZ> Kudos on trying to help them with the basics. It definitely takes a special kind of person to be awesome at customer service. (That's what I've been doing nearly 20 years ...and I hate talking on the phone)

One thing that could be useful if you haven't tried yet is role-playing. And recommending therapy for the issues causing him to take stuff personally, which could just be youth but the sooner to learn that skill,  the better equipped he'll be for life in general!

I tend to agree with <@U03K4PQJUCC> though. Customer service is kind of a dead-end job with not much of a path for advancement usually. If he's struggling with the basics (empathy/listening, being thick-skinned, patience, etc), I don't think he'd be a good fit.

For me, growing up catering to a narcissistic parent helped me learn skills required to deal with the most difficult of people and keep my head. So see? There's a plus. But i still hate phones.

query:
I'm conducting a comprehensive analysis of customer review acquisition strategies and their efficacy within B2B SaaS support organizations, specifically examining methodologies that have been empirically tested in production environments. I'm particularly interested in understanding:

(1) The correlation between post-interaction review solicitation timing and response rates
(2) The ethical implications and conversion impact of incentivization models (specifically non-monetary incentives such as environmental contributions versus traditional discount structures)
(3) The balance between maintaining authenticity perception while systematically requesting reviews as part of standardized support workflows

Context: I'm evaluating a proposal from our Customer Experience team at a mid-market data processing SaaS company (Datamolino) to implement a formalized review collection program. The proposed approach involves:
- Triggering review requests following NPS scores ≥9
- Post-resolution requests after support interactions rated positively
- Non-monetary incentive structure (tree planting initiative rather than vouchers/discounts)

What I need to determine: Has anyone documented their experience implementing similar review acquisition programs within their support or CX function, including both successful implementations and failed experiments? I'm specifically looking for data points on what methodologies yielded measurable increases in review volume while maintaining review authenticity and compliance with platform terms of service.

[Message by unknown at 87e10ff6-b76d-5472-9dc2-237c799fcd24]
Hi everyone! I’m sure this community has seen and tried it all when it comes to support tools, so I’m hoping you can help me out.
We’re exploring options to implement a conversational bot at EasyBroker, the SaaS company I work at, and would love your input.
Here’s what we’re looking for:
• A solid *conversational bot* to handle common questions
• *Smooth handoff to human agents* when needed
• *API integrations* to personalize responses based on the customer
• A focus on *great customer experience*, not just deflecting tickets
• The ability to *analyze team performance*, with clear separation between bot and human replies
Here are a few tools we’ve explored so far:
• *Chatbase / Botpress*: Great bot building capabilities, but no native handoff to humans
• *Help Scout*: Love the simplicity, but lacks external API access and user context
• *Tidio*: Checks many boxes, but the single-thread chat makes it hard to track and evaluate agent performance
• *Intercom*: Seems to do everything, but pricing is a concern
• *Crisp*: Interesting, but felt a bit rigid and robotic in conversation design
• *Zendesk / Freshdesk*: Powerful, but felt a bit heavy for our day-to-day needs
If you’ve found a tool that offers a good balance of bot flexibility, handoff, reporting, and usability—ideally without being overly complex or expensive—I’d really appreciate your recommendations.
Thanks so much in advance!

[Message by unknown at 042308be-06b3-5eff-b839-35038b4a56c4]
Wondering what you all make of this. A friend of mine recently told me about how he had an experience where he first went through a self serve chatbot that was clearly an AI, and when that bot couldn't solve his problem, connected him with 'agent Melvin'. He said that it looked like he spoke to a human, who gave him very clipped and bordering on rude answers (they were very to the point and lacked empathy that you'd expect from a person, especially in support). The cause for him contacting support later turned into a legal issue, where the conversation with 'Melvin' was referenced. In that reference, it turned out that 'Melvin' was indeed another chat bot, and my friend hadn't spoken to another human being at all.

The #sd-community-updates channel has been classified as "Internal - Moderate Sensitivity" per our data classification policy (DCP-2023-005).

**Specific Requirements:**
I need to identify and document:
- All user join events in #sd-community-updates channel
- All user departure events from #sd-community-updates channel  
- Timestamp information for each membership change (ISO 8601 format preferred)
- User IDs for cross-referencing with our identity management system

**Question:**
What is the complete chronological record of all membership changes (joins and departures) that occurred in the #sd-community-updates Slack channel, including user identifiers and message IDs for audit trail purposes?

We’ve created a bookmark folder so you can quickly access everyone’s posts. No hunting. No tab chaos. Just click, comment, and connect. :sparkles:

Not sure how to import a bookmark folder into Chrome? We’ve got you covered with a quick infographic to walk you through it (because let’s be honest, no one wants to Google that right now).

:pushpin: We’ll be updating this every month - so if you’ve got feedback or ideas to make it better, let us know!

Let’s keep growing this together without the cringe.

Excited to see everyone next week! As you’re exploring the schedule, I’d love if you joined us for any Conversation Corner session that interests you. Here’s what we’ll be talking about over the two days, and we’ll have speakers joining us for some sessions…

Monday
10-10:50 _*What have you learned from the early days of AI?*_
Is there anything that you’ve learned in the last 12 to 18 months about AI and how it affects your role and team? How have you evolved prepping your knowledge base for AI? Or other ways you’ve used it to interact with your customers? What mistakes have you learned from that you would like to share with others?

11-11:50 _*Evolving your career beyond the queue*_
Has your role grown beyond the queue? With AI, we have to evolve our careers into other areas of support, maybe even create new avenues. As the industry grows and changes, we also need to evolve with it. (w/<@U04MXEXABF1>)

2-2:50 _*Support teams & QA*_
Support leaders usually have a sense that improving QA can give us huge wins, but it’s often hard to prioritize, expensive, and easy to bump to “later.” Let’s share our wins and problem-solve together. (w/<@UBCEN768K>)

3-3:50 _*What does ops look like on your team?*_
Every support team needs operations. But what does that mean? What skills might you need to take on some of those needs for your team? And how can operations help with the overall business? (w/<@U01F6AWL45T>)

4-4:30 _*Job search support group*_ 
On the hunt for a new role? Or just want to chat about the current job landscape? Join us to swap interview tips, resume best practices, and ask any job seeking questions you might have to others.

Tuesday
9-9:50 _*How does your team operate?*_ 
Every support team operates a bit differently. If you have ever wanted to learn how other teams work and ask questions, join us and learn from each other.

10-10:50 _*LinkedIn and personal branding (Let’s connect!)*_
LinkedIn becomes more important every day as the support job landscape quickly changes. It feels more important than ever to cultivate a bit of a personal brand and let that come through in your LinkedIn profile. What has worked for you? What do you wish you knew about how LinkedIn can best work for you? (w/<@U08GLLA74DA>)

11-11:50 _*How to pivot from “support as a cost center” to “support as a value driver?”*_
Support will always be looked at as a cost center to leadership. But how can we shift that mindset? Has anything specific worked for you? Or what hasn’t quite worked?

Rescued a young squirrel that had been stuck between our fence (a section that used to be a dog run before we owned the place and had plywood panels) and our neighbors. Poor thing had been chirping off and on for a couple days - our little dog had been obsessed with it. It was right in a corner, and our yard backs up to an open space that has a different fence, and the chirping was coming from the corner so it was hard to tell where the critter was. My wife drove around to the open-space side but didn't see anything, but there's a fair amount of cactus up against the fence on that side so couldn't be sure. So I pulled out some rusty old screws and pried off a big plywood panel with a crowbar (there were also tacks or something holding it up that couldn't be seen, and some of the screws were so old and rusted that I couldn't unscrew them).

Anyway, the little squirrel raced out of there as soon as I'd opened it up enough, so hopefully it was just tired, hungry, thirsty and scared, and not actually injured.

But also, we had to put our big dog to sleep a few weeks ago, and that's been a hard adjustment. She was the best good girl.

Can I celebrate here a little? Rico let me brush him today! He came to us in January, abandoned, starved, and terrified after his owner was killed. We introduced him to dog food (he'd been eating scraps his whole life), taught him about beds, and blankets, and routines. He was sort of trained, but he's really a naturally eager-to-please mutt. He got over his fear of feet (mostly), and then his fear of doors. But brushing was one that he still struggled with even a month ago. If he saw a brush in our hands, he would whimper and run, then not come out of hiding until plied with treats. Mimi made it a sort of mission this summer to work on it.

They used a lot of treats and loves to get him used to seeing the brush, being near the brush, etc. We switched to a soft mitt and that seemed to make a huge difference. Today, with a steady stream of treats from Mimi, he let us brush him. With a small brush! He didn't love-love it, but he put up with it. Which is fantastic because boy howdy that boy can shed!
